In practice, synthetic genomic data should achieve a balance between privacy protection and data utility. While the PRISM-G score quantifies privacy risk, the usefulness of a synthetic dataset depends on its ability to preserve the statistical properties required for downstream analyses.

In this tutorial, we illustrate how to construct a privacy–utility frontier using genetic ancestry prediction as an example application. The objective is to compare different synthetic data generators according to the trade-off between their privacy risk and their ability to preserve population genetic structure.

For this evaluation, we first perform principal component analysis (PCA) on the 1000 Genomes Project genotype data to identify population clusters. The resulting principal components are then used as features to train a Random Forest classifier using the corresponding superpopulation labels. The trained model is subsequently applied to the synthetic datasets following a Train-on-Real, Test-on-Synthetic (TRTS) protocol to evaluate how well ancestry information is preserved.

The superpopulation classes in the 1000 Genomes Project are:

  • AFR — African
  • AMR — Admixed American
  • EAS — East Asian
  • EUR — European
  • SAS — South Asian

PCA analysis¶

def run_pca(geno_std, n_components=10):
    """
    Run PCA on standardized genotype matrix.
    Returns:
      pcs: (n_samples, n_components)
      pca_model: fitted PCA object
    """
    pca = PCA(n_components=n_components)
    pcs = pca.fit_transform(geno_std)
    return pcs, pca

pcs, pca_model = run_pca(real_std_G, n_components=10)

pc_cols = [f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(pcs.shape[1])]
pca_df = pd.DataFrame(
    pcs,
    index=real_samples,
    columns=pc_cols
)

# Add labels
pca_df["Population"] = meta["Population"].values
pca_df["Superpopulation"] = meta["Superpopulation"].values

datasets = {
    "gan": (gan_std_G, gan_samples),
    "rbm": (rbm_std_G, rbm_samples),
    "genom_h1": (genom_h1_std_G, genom_h1_samples),
    "genom_h10": (genom_h10_std_G, genom_h10_samples),
    "genom_h50": (genom_h50_std_G, genom_h50_samples),
    "safe": (safe_std_G, safe_samples),
    "leaky": (leaky_G, leaky_samples),
}

pca_dfs = {}

for name, (G, samples) in datasets.items():
    pcs = pca_model.transform(G)

    pca_dfs[name] = pd.DataFrame(
        pcs,
        index=samples,
        columns=[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(pcs.shape[1])]
    )

Utility metrics¶

We define two complementary utility metrics for this downstream application:

  • Population structure fidelity: It evaluates whether the global genetic structure of the synthetic dataset resembles that of the real cohort. Genotypes from the real cohort are first projected onto a principal component space, and the synthetic samples are projected using the same PCA model. Population centroids are then computed for each superpopulation, and the similarity between the real and synthetic centroid configurations is quantified using Procrustes similarity. A value close to 1 indicates that the synthetic data preserve the overall ancestry structure, whereas values closer to 0 indicate substantial distortion of the population geometry.

  • Ancestry prediction similarity: It evaluates whether the synthetic dataset supports ancestry prediction comparable to the real data. A Random Forest classifier is trained using the principal components of the real training cohort and the corresponding superpopulation labels. The trained classifier is then applied to the synthetic samples, and the predicted ancestry proportions are compared with those observed in the real cohort. Similarity is quantified using the Jensen–Shannon (JS) similarity, defined as

    $$ \mathrm{JS}_{\mathrm{sim}} = 1 - \mathrm{JS}(\pi_{\mathrm{real}}, \pi_{\mathrm{syn}}) $$

    where $\pi_{\mathrm{real}}$ and $\pi_{\mathrm{syn}}$ denote the ancestry distributions of the real and synthetic datasets, respectively.

    Higher values indicate that the synthetic dataset preserves the ancestry composition required for downstream prediction tasks.

In [8]:
Copied! 
def kl_divergence(p, q, eps=1e-12, base=2):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    p = p / (p.sum() + eps)
    q = q / (q.sum() + eps)
    p = np.clip(p, eps, 1.0)
    q = np.clip(q, eps, 1.0)
    log = np.log if base is None else (lambda x: np.log(x) / np.log(base))
    return np.sum(p * (log(p) - log(q)))

def js_divergence(p, q, eps=1e-12, base=2):
    p = np.asarray(p, dtype=float)
    q = np.asarray(q, dtype=float)
    p = p / (p.sum() + eps)
    q = q / (q.sum() + eps)
    m = 0.5 * (p + q)
    return 0.5 * kl_divergence(p, m, eps=eps, base=base) + 0.5 * kl_divergence(q, m, eps=eps, base=base)

def mixture_js_from_classifier(real_pcs, real_labels, syn_pcs, base=2):
    y_real = np.asarray(real_labels)
    pops = np.unique(y_real)

    clf = RandomForestClassifier(
        n_estimators=500,
        random_state=0,
        n_jobs=-1,
        class_weight="balanced_subsample",
    )
    clf.fit(real_pcs, y_real)

    # Real proportions
    pi_real = np.array([(y_real == p).mean() for p in pops])

    # Soft mixture on synthetic
    proba_syn = clf.predict_proba(syn_pcs)
    idx = np.array([np.where(clf.classes_ == p)[0][0] for p in pops])
    proba_syn = proba_syn[:, idx]
    pi_syn = proba_syn.mean(axis=0)

    y_syn_pred = clf.predict(syn_pcs)
    return clf, pops, pi_real, pi_syn, y_syn_pred, proba_syn

def procrustes_on_centroids(real_pcs, real_labels, syn_pcs, syn_labels_pred, dims=(0,1)):
    Xr = real_pcs[:, list(dims)]
    Xs = syn_pcs[:, list(dims)]

    y_real = np.asarray(real_labels)
    y_syn  = np.asarray(syn_labels_pred)

    pops = np.unique(y_real)

    # Centroids: K x 2
    C_real = np.vstack([Xr[y_real == p].mean(axis=0) for p in pops])
    C_syn  = np.vstack([Xs[y_syn  == p].mean(axis=0) for p in pops])

    ok = ~np.isnan(C_syn).any(axis=1)
    C_real = C_real[ok]
    C_syn  = C_syn[ok]
    pops_ok = pops[ok]

    if len(pops_ok) <= 2:
        similarity = 0.0
        disparity = 1.0
        return similarity, disparity, pops_ok, C_real, C_syn
 
    _, _, disparity = procrustes(C_real, C_syn)
    similarity = 1.0 - disparity

    return similarity, disparity, pops_ok, C_real, C_syn

real_pcs = pca_df[[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(10)]].values
real_labels = pca_df["Superpopulation"].values

results = {}

for name, syn_df in pca_dfs.items():

    syn_pcs = syn_df[[f"PC{i+1}" for i in range(10)]].values

    # Classifier-based mixture estimation
    clf, pops, pi_real, pi_syn, y_syn_pred, proba_syn = mixture_js_from_classifier(
        real_pcs,
        real_labels,
        syn_pcs,
    )

    js = js_divergence(pi_real, pi_syn)

    # Procrustes on inferred ancestry centroids
    proc_similarity, proc_disparity, pops_ok, C_real, C_syn = (
        procrustes_on_centroids(
            real_pcs,
            real_labels,
            syn_pcs,
            y_syn_pred,
        )
    )

    results[name] = {
        "classifier": clf,
        "populations": pops,
        "pi_real": pi_real,
        "pi_syn": pi_syn,
        "js": js,
        "js_similarity": 1.0 - js,
        "predicted_labels": y_syn_pred,
        "probabilities": proba_syn,
        "procrustes_similarity": proc_similarity,
        "procrustes_disparity": proc_disparity,
        "centroid_populations": pops_ok,
        "real_centroids": C_real,
        "synthetic_centroids": C_syn,
    }

To summarize utility in a single value, we compute the utility metric as the mean of the two metrics:

$$ U = \frac{\mathrm{Procrustes}_{\mathrm{sim}} + \mathrm{JS}_{\mathrm{sim}}}{2}. $$

This score ranges from 0 to 1, with larger values indicating better preservation of both population structure and ancestry prediction performance.

Constructing the Privacy–Utility Frontier¶

The privacy–utility frontier is obtained by plotting each synthetic generator according to

  • x-axis: Utility score
  • y-axis: (100 - PRISM-G privacy score)

Each point represents one synthetic dataset, allowing direct comparison of different generative models.

Datasets located toward the upper-right corner simultaneously achieve high utility and low privacy risk, whereas datasets in the lower-left corner exhibit poor utility and/or increased privacy exposure.

The frontier can be used to identify generators that provide the most favorable balance between privacy preservation and downstream analytical performance.

In [10]:
Copied! 
methods = ["Safe","GAN","Genomator (H=1)","Genomator (H=10)",
          "Genomator (H=50)","RBM","Leaky"]
prismg = [0,28.289,48.780,47.162,43.970,69.734,100]
utility = [39.636, 95.641,99.777,99.693,99.754,95.832,96.363]

# 1. Rescale privacy: 100 = Safe, 0 = Leaky
privacy_score = [100 - p for p in prismg]

points = list(zip(methods, privacy_score, utility))

# 2. Compute Pareto front (maximize utility AND privacy_score)
def dominates(p, q):
    # p, q: (name, privacy_score, utility)
    return (p[1] >= q[1] and p[2] >= q[2]) and (p[1] > q[1] or p[2] > q[2])

pareto = []
for i, p in enumerate(points):
    if not any(dominates(points[j], p) for j in range(len(points)) if j != i):
        pareto.append(p)

# Sort Pareto points by utility (x-axis)
pareto_sorted = sorted(pareto, key=lambda x: x[2])

# 3. Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(7,4))

# Plot ALL points but distinguish Pareto vs non-Pareto
for (m, ps, u) in points:
    if (m, ps, u) in pareto:
        plt.scatter(u, ps, color="orange", marker='o', s=80)   # Pareto point
    else:
        plt.scatter(u, ps, color="gray", marker='x', s=70)      # Non-Pareto point
    plt.annotate(m, (u, ps), textcoords="offset points", xytext=(4,3), fontsize=8)

# Draw Pareto front
pf_x = [u for (_, _, u) in pareto_sorted]
pf_y = [ps for (_, ps, _) in pareto_sorted]
plt.plot(pf_x, pf_y, linestyle='--', color='orange')

plt.xlabel("Utility (Mean performance metrics)")
plt.ylabel("Privacy (100 - PRISM-G score)")
plt.title("")
plt.grid(True)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
